noi_dung:
In Cultivating the Way, Do Not Compete

Now in the Chan Session, practitioners apply effort—but a shallow skill. People treat Chan like a race, vying for first. You can sit three hours—I'll sit five, a cut above you. With such a mind in Chan, how could you awaken? Though you sat for eighty thousand great kalpas, you could never understand the mind and see the nature. Why? Only because you harbor a winning-losing mind. There is a saying:

Fighting comes from a winning-losing mind;

It runs counter to the Way.

Four marks arising in the mind—

How attain samadhi?

These four verses warn cultivators never to give rise to contention. When skill is complete, wisdom appears—and others will naturally rank you first. That is true first place. But craving first place in your heart—that is a winning-losing mind, running counter to the Way.

Cultivators must be like water. Water's nature is yielding—claiming no merit, grasping no virtue—giving what is good to others, keeping what is bad for itself. Laozi said: Supreme good is like water. Water benefits the myriad things without contending. Water dwells where all disdain to dwell—hence it accords with the Way."

Supreme good describes supreme practitioners. They are likened to water. Water flows to low places, benefiting all things without contending for merit or virtue. Toward every kind—birds, fish and shrimp, beasts or plants, whether womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, or transformation-born—water treats all alike, giving equally to all. Cultivators are the same—toward all beings as past parents, as future Buddhas. Cultivators must spread kind hearts, finding means to rescue beings from the sea of suffering—dwelling where beings refuse to dwell. With such thoughts, the practitioner nears the Way. But a winning-losing mind runs counter to the cultivator's principles—against the Way.

Cultivators must be free of the four marks.

Who cultivates? Sensing no one cultivating—that is no mark of self.

Sensing no winning or losing with anyone—that is no mark of others.

Seeing neither self's mark nor others' mark—naturally the mark of living beings is also gone.

With no mark of living beings, whence a mark of life? Thus no mark of a life.

Harboring thoughts of vying to win, the four marks surely follow; with the four marks, samadhi can never be reached. This principle we must practice and polish well. In short, whoever retains the four marks is a common being; whoever is free of the four marks is a Bodhisattva.

Cultivators must remember the four verses in the Diamond Sutra:

All conditioned dharmas

Are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, shadows;

Like dew and lightning—

Contemplate them thus.

Whatever has shape and marks is a conditioned dharma. Conditioned dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a water bubble, a shadow, a lightning flash—all hollow, without substance. Contemplate all things thus—only then can the true principle be clearly understood, clinging ended, discursive thoughts no longer troubling us.

The Diamond Sutra further says: "The past mind cannot be grasped, the present mind cannot be grasped, the future mind cannot be grasped." Why cannot the past mind be grasped? Because the past is gone—why mind it? Why cannot the present mind be grasped? Because in the present, thoughts succeed unbroken. You call this the present—but spoken, that present is already gone; time never pauses. Why cannot the future mind be grasped? Because the future has not yet come. So past, present, future—these three minds cannot be grasped. Practicing per the Buddha's teaching, you may at once reach the state of Nirvana.

Cultivators of the Way must take right knowledge and views as their model for vigorous practice. In practice, "apart from the mark of speech"—for nothing remains to say; "apart from the mark of mind's conditions"—for no conditions remain for the mind to chase; "apart from the mark of words"—for no words remain to describe. Unspeakable—what remains to remember? What can we still not let go? What remains to concern us? Friends! Apply effort right there—instead of shallow effort on the outer shell!

Someone thinks: "Today in Chan, my legs didn't hurt, my back didn't ache—I didn't even hear the rest bell." That means he dozed off—of course knowing nothing. Do not mistake that state, lest you go astray and fall under demonic influence!

Take heed! Meeting strange states in Chan investigation, pay them no mind, no attention—let them be naturally, unmoved by strange states. The Shurangama Sutra explains this most clearly. May practitioners study its "Fifty Skandha-Demons" thoroughly.

The Shurangama Sutra is a precious mirror for Chan investigators—so all cultivators must ponder this Sutra deeply.
